newsitem.title: USA: Forbes leads Republicans against budget deal.
newsitem.headline: Forbes leads Republicans against budget deal.

text.p: Millionaire publisher Steve Forbes, who ran unsuccessfully for the Republican presidential nomination last year, on Thursday launched a radio advertising campaign against a budget deal taking shape between President Clinton and congressional Republicans.
The Clinton Administration and congressional Republicans were close to a pact to balance the budget by 2002 but were still wrangling about Medicare cost reduction and details of tax cuts.

Forbes, who has formed an organisation called "Americans for Hope, Growth and Opportunity", released the text of three radio ads to be aired in the Washington D.C. area, clearly aimed at influencing Republicans to rebel against the deal.
"Clinton's budget is really a $23 billion tax increase. Promising a tax cut when it's really a tax increase -- that's Clintonomics," said one ad.

"It's time to pass an honest budget, with a big income tax cut. Let's help families keep more of what they earn, help our economy grow and create new revenue to help balance the budget," said another.

Forbes' broadside appeared to be an early sign of discontent among Republican fiscal conservatives at the deal taking shape. He was a signatory Wednesday of a letter to House Speaker Newt Gingrich and Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott objecting to the deal.
Defeated Republican vice presidential candidate Jack Kemp also signed the letter.
Kemp and Forbes both appear to be positioning themselves for presidential runs in 2000.
While Republican leaders will have difficulty winning support for the deal, Clinton also faces problems from House Democrats who have objected to deep domestic spending cuts.
Budget talks were to continue on Thursday. Clinton has said he hoped to conclude an agreement before leaving on Monday for Mexico.

The two sides have been negotiating for weeks on a plan to wipe out the deficit by 2002. The size of tax cuts, spending cuts and the president's request for some new programmes have been the major divisions.
